name: Gender-neutral aesthetics / 'pretty boy' / softboy

card.summary: A soft, androgynous look built through skincare, hair, grooming and styling to emphasize delicate features.

quick.overview:
This aesthetic aims for soft, delicate, androgynous features in men instead of heavy masculine angularity.

People pursue it with skincare, hair, grooming, makeup and clothing.
quick.mechanism: Followers emphasize smooth skin, eyes, lips and styled hair, and choose clothing and grooming that read as soft and polished.
quick.risks: Mostly styling choices; any procedures people pair with it carry their own risks.

lead: Gender-neutral, "pretty boy" or softboy aesthetics describe a look built on soft, delicate or androgynous features in men: clear skin, expressive eyes and lashes, fuller lips, a gentler jawline and well-kept hair, rather than heavy, angular dimorphism. People pursue it through skincare, hair, grooming, eye and lash care, makeup, fashion and sometimes facial procedures, and it is an alternative route to looking attractive for those who do not aim for a "chad" build. [1][4][5]

The look has long precedent in popular culture, from 1970s glam figures such as David Bowie and Marc Bolan to Prince and Boy George, and Japanese and Korean pop culture has treated androgynous looks as a positive attribute. [1] In Japan the ideal of the bishonen (beautiful youth) is central to manga, anime and idol culture and has roots reaching back centuries. [2] In South Korea the related kkonminam ("flower handsome man") image, used since the late 1990s, centres on attractive young men who invest in grooming, fashion and cosmetics. [3]

On looksmax.org, "pretty boy" is a recurring archetype that members compare with "chad" and discuss in threads about hair, eyes, skin and style. [4][5] The look is mainly a styling and grooming approach; no clinical research addresses it as such.

chain: Prioritise skin, hair, lashes and grooming
Softer, more harmonious and polished features
angle.text: Followers use skincare, haircare, grooming, eye and lash care, makeup and styling to emphasise smooth skin and delicate features. It is a styling approach rather than a single product, and the same tools are available to anyone regardless of bone structure.

infobox: Androgyny, softboy, pretty boy, bishonen, kkonminam (flower boy) [2][3]
Skincare, hair, lashes and brows, grooming, makeup, fashion
Glam rock, Japanese bishonen, Korean flower boys, K-pop and J-pop [1][2][3]

paras: The aesthetic emphasises softness: clear skin, expressive eyes, fuller lips, styled hair and a less pronounced jaw. Practitioners adapt fashion and grooming to match, including jewelry, makeup and unisex clothing, which became mainstream in men's fashion in the West and Asia. [1]

In a looksmax.org thread asking what pretty-boy aesthetics are, replies listed hair, long eyelashes, skin and good style, with one also naming facial width-to-height ratio, a pointed chin and "doe eyes". [5] A multi-part "pretty boy guide" on the same forum begins with the eye area, covering lash growth and lifting, conditioning serums and light eyeliner for those whose look suits it. [4]

Androgynous fashion appears across the twentieth century, from 1920s flappers and Marlene Dietrich to Yves Saint Laurent's 1966 tuxedo suit, Bowie's Ziggy Stardust in 1972, and 1980s figures such as Prince and Boy George. [1]

Bishonen ("beautiful youth") is a Japanese term for a young man of androgynous beauty, with an aesthetic described as central to shojo manga and anime, popular with girls and women, and embodied by many idols from the talent agency Johnny & Associates. [2] The page describes the term as emerging in the Meiji era and androgynous glam rock in the 1970s as boosting the look's popularity. [2]

Kkonminam has been used since the late 1990s for attractive young men who focus on style, grooming and fashion, often including cosmetics. [3] Late-1990s advertising and dramas replaced tough male images with men with smooth, fair skin and silky hair, and the 2009 drama Boys Over Flowers is credited with encouraging many men to take their appearance more seriously. [3] Global K-pop fans use the "flower boy" label for Korean male idols. [3]

timeline.event: Writer Kyokutei Bakin uses the word bishonen in a work about the younger partner in a male relationship. [2]
Yves Saint Laurent introduces the women's tuxedo suit Le Smoking. [1]
David Bowie's Ziggy Stardust persona becomes a symbol of sexual ambiguity. [1]
Kkonminam imagery becomes prominent in Korean entertainment. [3]
Boys Over Flowers popularises the flower boy look. [3]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the pretty-boy look is discussed as a target that members optimise with skin, hair, lashes and styling, often set against the "chad" archetype. [4][5]

claims.claim: Skin, hair, lashes and style define the pretty-boy look
claims.believers: Forum members list hair, long eyelashes, skin and good style as the core traits, with some adding doe eyes and a pointed chin. [5]
claims.experts: No published studies have examined this specific aesthetic; cultural histories describe smooth skin, groomed hair and cosmetics as common to bishonen and kkonminam looks. [2][3]

claims.claim: The eye area is the first priority for the look
claims.believers: A multi-part forum guide starts with lashes, lash serums and lifts, and light eyeliner for some users. [4]
claims.experts: No published studies have compared eye-area grooming approaches for this aesthetic.
